steps.title: What the appraising exam actually asks
steps.body:
Music is three components, and only one of them is an exam.

- **Performing** (30%) and **Composing** (30%) are coursework, done in lessons and marked by the school.
- **Appraising** (40%) is the written paper, and it is the only part this app can help with.

The paper is **1 hour 45 minutes** and **80 marks**:

- **Section A, 68 marks.** Six questions on six of the eight set works, plus a short melody or rhythm **dictation**. Extracts are played several times.
- **Section B, 12 marks.** One extended **comparison** between a set work and an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study, with skeleton scores for both.

So a set work has to be known well enough for two different jobs: answering detailed questions about it, and holding it up against something you have never heard.

One practical point that shapes everything below: you cannot revise music by reading about it. Play the recording, and map the structure yourself while it runs.

visuals.alt: A table of the three components of Edexcel GCSE Music with their weighting and how each is assessed

check.prompt: How many marks is Section B worth?
check.solution: Section B is **12** of the 80 marks: one extended comparison. Section A carries the other 68.

steps.title: The elements you describe music with
steps.body:
Every answer in this paper is written in the language of the **musical elements**. Learn them as a checklist, because when a question asks *how* a composer does something, the answer is always one or more of these.

- **Melody**: the tune. Steps or leaps, range, sequence, ornament, riff.
- **Harmony and tonality**: the chords and the key. Major or minor, cadences, modulation.
- **Rhythm and metre**: the pulse. Time signature, syncopation, dotted rhythms, triplets.
- **Texture**: how many layers and how they relate. Monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic.
- **Timbre and instrumentation**: what is playing, and the quality of its sound.
- **Dynamics and articulation**: loud and soft, smooth and detached.
- **Structure**: the order of sections.
- **Tempo**: the speed.

A useful discipline: never write a sentence about a piece that could not be pinned to one of these words.

steps.title: Killer Queen: the facts to know cold
steps.body:
Written by **Freddie Mercury**, recorded by **Queen**, released in **1974** on the album *Sheer Heart Attack*. It is one of the two **vocal music** set works, the other being Purcell's *Music for a While* — which is who you may be asked to compare it with.

The basics:

- **Key**: E flat major, moving through related keys.
- **Metre**: **12/8** — compound quadruple, so each of the four beats divides into three. That is where the lilt comes from.
- **Tempo**: moderate, around 116 beats per minute.
- **Structure**: intro, verse–chorus twice, guitar solo, verse–chorus, fade.
- **Forces**: lead vocal, layered backing vocals, electric guitars, bass, drums, piano.

And the detail examiners love: the sleeve of Queen albums of this period stated **no synthesisers**. Every sound that resembles one is a guitar, a voice or a piano, treated in the studio. That single fact explains a great deal about how the record was made.

steps.title: The structure, section by section
steps.body:
This is the part that cannot be done by reading. Learn the order below, then put the studio recording on and hear it go past. Do it three or four times over the course of the topic and the structure stops being a list and becomes something you can hear coming.

There are no timings here on purpose. Recordings differ, and a map you make yourself while listening is worth far more than one you read. The your-turn step asks you to make it.

What to listen for as you go:

- The **intro** has no drums. Voice and piano only, and it is deliberately thin.
- The **first chorus** is where the multitracked vocals arrive. Notice how much bigger it suddenly is.
- The **guitar solo** replaces what could have been a third verse, and it is in harmony with itself.
- The song **fades** rather than ending on a chord.

steps.title: The studio as an instrument
steps.body:
The single most examinable thing about this song is **how it was made**. Queen treat the studio as an instrument, and three techniques do most of the work.

**Multitracking**, also called overdubbing: a part is recorded, then recorded again on top, many times. The vocal harmonies are layered until four singers sound like a choir. Because the intro is so thin, that thickening at the chorus is the song's biggest single effect.

**Guitar overdubs**: Brian May plays the solo in harmony **with himself**, so one guitarist produces a three-part texture. It functions rather like a brass section, and it cannot be played live by one person as recorded.

**Panning, delay and reverb**: sounds are placed across the stereo field and given depth. Panning is what keeps so many layers from turning to mud.

In an exam, none of these earns a mark on its own. Name the device, then say **what it does to the sound**.

visuals.problem: Turning a technique into an answer

steps.text: *They use multitracking.* — names a device, no effect, low mark
*The vocals are multitracked.* — slightly better, still no consequence
steps.note: A list of features is not an explanation

steps.text: *The vocal harmonies are multitracked, so four singers sound like a choir.* — device plus effect
*The vocal harmonies are multitracked, so four singers sound like a choir; because the intro is only voice and piano, that sudden weight is what makes the chorus land.*
steps.note: Device, effect, and where it happens: full marks

check.solution: Only the first names a **device** and ties it to an audible **effect**. The others are praise, a bare fact, and a description of the structure.

steps.title: Melody, harmony and rhythm
steps.body:
**Melody.** The vocal line is wide-ranging and often **syncopated**, landing off the beat so it pulls against the steady band. Mercury uses **falsetto** at the top of the range. The backing vocals move in **close harmony**, in blocks rather than as independent lines.

**Harmony and tonality.** E flat major, but it moves restlessly through related keys rather than sitting still. Among the cadences is an **interrupted cadence**, where chord V is followed by chord **vi** instead of the I the ear expects — a small surprise that keeps a phrase from closing too neatly. There are also chromatic chords borrowed from outside the key.

**Rhythm and metre.** **12/8**: four beats to a bar, each dividing into **three**. That is *compound* time, and it is unusual for a rock song, giving the track a rolling lilt instead of a square backbeat. Against that, the syncopated vocal keeps the surface unpredictable.

**Texture.** Mostly **homophonic** — a melody with accompaniment — though the density changes enormously between the intro and the choruses.

check.prompt: What does it mean that the song is in a **compound** metre?
check.solution: **Compound** describes how the beat divides: into **three** rather than two. 12/8 is four beats, each of three quavers, which is what gives the lilt.

steps.title: Your turn: listen and place the sections
steps.body:
Play the studio recording on whatever the family uses. On paper, copy the table below and write the time each section starts as you hear it arrive. Then play it again and check: the second listen is where you hear sections coming that you missed the first time.

The things worth catching by ear, in order of difficulty:

1. The moment the drums enter, which is not at the start.
2. The jump in texture at the first chorus.
3. The guitar solo arriving where a verse would have been.
4. The fade, rather than a final chord.

When you can hear all four coming, you know the structure well enough for Section A.

steps.title: Grade 9: the comparison, and how to answer a how question
steps.body:
Two habits carry the top marks in this paper.

**Answer a *how* question with a device and an effect.** *How does the composer create excitement?* is not asking what happens; it is asking what causes it. The shape is: **the effect**, **the device that produces it**, **where it happens**. A list of features with no consequences sits in the bottom band however accurate it is.

**Organise Section B by element, not by piece.** This is the single commonest way to lose marks in the whole paper. Compare melody in both pieces, then rhythm in both, then texture in both. Writing everything about piece A and then everything about piece B leaves the examiner to do the comparing, and a comparison mark scheme cannot award that.

For *Killer Queen* the likely partner is Purcell's *Music for a While*, the other vocal music set work, and the contrast is unusually rich: a studio construction against a piece written for live performance; layered close harmony against a solo voice over a ground bass; a syncopated wide-ranging line against stepwise Baroque writing with word painting.

And finish Section B with a **judgement**. Not which is better, but what the differences *do*: Queen use the voice as a material to build with, Purcell uses it to deliver a text.

rows: ties each feature to its effect
bar numbers from the skeleton score

steps.text: *Killer Queen has multitracked vocals. Music for a While has one voice.* — two facts, no comparison
*Where Queen layer multitracked close harmony into blocks, Purcell sets a single voice over a ground bass…*
steps.note: Both pieces in one sentence, on one element

steps.text: *…so Queen's texture is dense and manufactured while Purcell's stays transparent and can be followed line by line.*
That last clause is the judgement, and it is what reaches level 4
steps.note: Say what the difference does, not just that it exists

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **The paper**: Appraising, 1 h 45, **80 marks**, 40% of the GCSE. Section A **68** marks, six set works plus dictation; Section B **12** marks, one comparison.
- **Killer Queen**: Freddie Mercury, recorded by Queen, **1974**, *Sheer Heart Attack*. Area of study: **vocal music**.
- **Key** E flat major, **metre 12/8** compound quadruple, moderate tempo.
- **Structure**: intro (no drums), verse–chorus twice, **guitar solo**, verse–chorus, **fade**.
- **Technology is the point**: multitracked close-harmony vocals, guitar overdubbed in harmony with itself, panning, delay and reverb. Famously **no synthesisers**.
- **Melody** syncopated and wide-ranging, with **falsetto**; **texture** homophonic but hugely variable in density; an **interrupted cadence** (V to vi) among the harmony.
- **A *how* question** wants the effect, the device that causes it, and where it happens.
- **Section B** is organised **by element**, covering both pieces in each paragraph, and ends with a judgement about what the differences do.
- **You cannot revise this by reading.** Play the 1974 studio recording and make your own map of the sections while it runs.

questions.prompt: Explain how Queen use music technology to create the sound of *Killer Queen*.
questions.solution: Named devices tied to their effect. Multitracking: the vocal harmonies are recorded many times and layered, so the chorus sounds like a choir rather than a band, and the contrast with the sparse intro is what makes the chorus land. Overdubbing on guitar: Brian May harmonises with himself, giving a three-part guitar texture no single take could produce. Panning, delay and reverb place sounds across the stereo field and give depth. Level 3 needs each device tied to an audible effect, not just listed.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): devices named with little or no effect given
Level 2 (3 to 4): some devices linked to their effect, with limited reference to the music
Level 3 (5 to 6): devices named, linked to their effect, and located in the song

criteria.text: Multitracking of the vocals named, and located in the chorus
Its effect explained: a choral weight far beyond four singers, contrasting with the sparse intro
Guitar overdubbing named, with Brian May harmonising with himself
A further effect such as panning, delay or reverb, with what it does to the stereo image or depth

questions.modelAnswer: Queen build the track in the studio rather than capturing a live performance. The vocal harmonies are **multitracked**, recorded many times over and layered, so the chorus has the weight of a choir even though there are only four members; because the intro is just voice and piano, that sudden thickening is what gives the chorus its impact. Brian May's guitar solo is **overdubbed** in harmony with himself, producing a three-part guitar texture that one player could never perform live in a single take, and which functions almost like a brass section. **Panning** moves sounds across the stereo field so the layers stay distinct rather than turning to mud, and **delay** and **reverb** add depth behind the voice. Together these mean the record is an object made in the studio, which is exactly what the sleeve note *no synthesisers* was drawing attention to.

questions.prompt: Why does the sparse intro matter to the effect of the first chorus?
questions.solution: The intro is voice and piano with no drums, so when the full multitracked band arrives the change in **texture** is dramatic. The key is major throughout, the tempo does not double, and the solo theme is not stated in the intro.

questions.prompt: Compare the use of voices in *Killer Queen* with that in a piece of Baroque vocal music such as Purcell's *Music for a While*. Refer to melody, texture and the role of technology.
questions.solution: Organised by element, both pieces in each paragraph, with a judgement at the end. Melody: Mercury's line is syncopated, wide-ranging and uses falsetto, while Purcell's is stepwise and ornamented with the word painting of the Baroque. Texture: Queen layer close harmony into blocks, Purcell sets a single voice over a ground bass and continuo. Technology: the whole of *Killer Queen* is a studio construction that cannot be performed live as recorded, while Purcell's piece is written to be performed live and technology plays no part in the composition.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 3): separate descriptions with few technical terms and no real comparison
Level 2 (4 to 6): some comparison, organised loosely, with some correct terminology
Level 3 (7 to 9): comparison organised by element, accurate terms, evidence from both pieces
Level 4 (10 to 12): sustained comparison by element throughout, with a judgement about the effect of the differences

criteria.text: Melody compared across both: syncopation, range and falsetto against stepwise Baroque writing with ornament and word painting
Texture compared: layered close harmony in blocks against a solo voice over ground bass and continuo
The role of technology compared: a studio construction against a piece written for live performance
A judgement about what the differences do to the listener, rather than a list of them

questions.modelAnswer: The two pieces use the voice for opposite purposes, and the differences run through every element. In **melody**, Mercury's line is wide-ranging and heavily syncopated, pushing against the beat, and rises into falsetto for its highest moments, so the voice sounds athletic and theatrical; Purcell's line is largely stepwise and ornamented, and it bends to the meaning of individual words, so the voice sounds declamatory and rhetorical rather than virtuosic. In **texture**, Queen stack multitracked close harmonies into solid blocks that move together, which makes four singers sound like a choir; Purcell places a single voice above a ground bass and continuo, so the texture stays transparent and the listener follows one line throughout. The **role of technology** is the deepest difference: *Killer Queen* is assembled in the studio from overdubs, panning and delay, and could not be reproduced live as it stands, whereas Purcell's piece is composed entirely for live performance and its effects come from harmony and word setting alone. The result is that Queen use the voice as one more material to be built with, while Purcell uses it to deliver a text, and that difference of purpose explains almost every surface difference between them.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of *Killer Queen* keeps a listener's interest across three minutes.
questions.solution: Devices tied to effect. The verse–chorus alternation gives returning familiarity; the sparse intro makes the first chorus land; the guitar solo breaks the pattern before a third verse could feel repetitive; the fade-out avoids a final cadence. Each point needs its consequence for the listener, not just its name.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): sections named with little effect given
Level 2 (3 to 4): some sections linked to their effect
Level 3 (5 to 6): several structural choices tied to their effect on the listener

criteria.text: Verse and chorus alternation named, with the effect of a familiar return
The contrast of the sparse intro with the full chorus, and what it does
The guitar solo placed before a third verse, breaking the pattern, or the fade-out avoiding a final cadence

questions.modelAnswer: The song alternates verse and chorus, so the listener always has something familiar returning, and the hook is heard three times without being stated continuously. The intro is deliberately thin, just voice and piano, so that when the full multitracked band arrives at the first chorus the jump in texture is dramatic rather than gradual. Before the pattern can wear out, the **guitar solo** replaces what would have been a third verse, changing the timbre and giving the voice a rest, and because it is overdubbed in harmony it brings a new texture rather than simply a new tune. Finally the song **fades** instead of cadencing, so it seems to continue beyond the record, which suits the ambiguity of the character being described.

examTechnique.body:
Only Component 3 is examined, so this is where revision goes. The paper rewards two different things: knowing each set work in detail for Section A, and being able to hold one up against an unfamiliar piece in Section B.

Section A questions are mostly short. One mark wants one term, correctly spelled; three marks want three separate points, not one point explained three times. Where a question asks *how* a composer achieves something, name the device and give its effect, because the effect is where the mark is.

Section B is worth 12 marks and is lost more often by structure than by knowledge. Organise by musical element, cover both pieces in every paragraph, quote bar numbers from the skeleton score, and end with a judgement about what the differences do.

And the practical point: play the recording and make your own map of the sections. This topic cannot be learnt from the page.
examinerErrors: Writing a paragraph on each piece in Section B instead of a paragraph on each element. A comparison mark scheme cannot reward two separate descriptions.
Answering a *how* question with a list of features and no effects. The device earns little; the consequence earns the mark.
Calling the chorus texture polyphonic. The layered vocals move together in blocks, so it is homophonic.
Describing 12/8 as simple time, or as three beats in a bar. It is four beats, each dividing into three: compound quadruple.
Saying a synthesiser produces the guitar-like sounds. Queen's sleeves of this period state no synthesisers, and the examiner is watching for it.
Writing praise rather than analysis: that the singing is powerful or the solo impressive. Neither is a musical observation.
Giving one developed point where three marks are offered. Three marks means three separate points.
Revising the song by reading about it. Section A plays the extract, so the structure has to be recognisable by ear.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer describes music in the language of the elements and never writes a sentence that could not be pinned to one of them. On a *how* question it names the effect, the device that produces it and where in the extract it happens. It knows the facts cold — 1974, E flat major, 12/8, verse and chorus with a solo and a fade — so no time is spent recalling them. In Section B it compares by element with both pieces in every paragraph, cites the skeleton score, and finishes with a judgement about what the differences do to a listener rather than stopping at the differences themselves.
